title: The computer that landed on the Moon had 4 KB of RAM
body: The Apollo Guidance Computer had about 4 kilobytes of working memory and 72 kilobytes of fixed memory. Its software was literally woven: workers threaded wires through tiny magnetic rings by hand to store each bit.
takeaway: Tight limits forced extremely careful engineering. The software held up when alarms fired during the landing.
visual: hands threading fine copper wire through rows of tiny rings, with the Moon visible through a window behind

title: The first computer "bug" was a real moth
body: On 9 September 1947, operators of Harvard's Mark II computer found a moth jammed in a relay. They taped it into the logbook with the note "First actual case of bug being found." Engineers had already used "bug" for faults since Edison's day.
takeaway: The logbook page, moth included, is kept at the Smithsonian.
source: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
visual: a moth taped to a yellowed lined logbook page beside banks of old electromechanical relays

title: Your keyboard layout was designed for 1870s machinery
body: QWERTY was developed by Christopher Latham Sholes for early typewriters, whose metal arms jammed when neighbouring ones were struck in quick succession. The machines are long gone, and the layout remains.
takeaway: Once everyone has learned a standard, even a better one struggles to replace it.
source: Paul David, "Clio and the Economics of QWERTY" (1985)
visual: a vintage typewriter with its fan of metal type arms raised, morphing on one side into a modern backlit keyboard

title: From 2,300 transistors to tens of billions
body: Intel's first microprocessor, the 4004 of 1971, had about 2,300 transistors. Today's largest chips carry tens of billions on a piece of silicon the size of a fingernail or a postage stamp.
takeaway: Gordon Moore predicted this doubling in 1965. It has held, roughly, for sixty years.
visual: a microchip seen from above as a vast glowing city grid at night, streets becoming finer and denser toward the centre

title: The internet runs along the sea floor
body: More than 95% of data crossing between continents travels through undersea fibre-optic cables, not satellites. There are over 500 of them, more than a million kilometres in all, most about as thick as a garden hose.
takeaway: "The cloud" is a physical network. Cut a few cables and a country can go dark.
visual: a thin glowing cable running across a dark ocean floor past a curious fish, light pulsing along its length

title: The web was given away for free
body: Tim Berners-Lee put the first website online at CERN in 1991. On 30 April 1993, CERN released the web's software into the public domain, with no fees and no patents.
takeaway: An open standard anyone could build on beat every closed network of its day.
visual: a single early-1990s computer on a plain desk, a web of glowing threads spreading outward from its screen to the whole world

title: Proving you were human digitised millions of books
body: The reCAPTCHA system showed people words that scanning software could not read. Each time someone typed one in, they helped transcribe old books and newspaper archives. Its inventor, Luis von Ahn, went on to found Duolingo.
takeaway: Ten seconds of effort, multiplied by millions of people a day, becomes real work.
visual: ribbons of wavy ink lifting off the pages of old books and straightening into neat parallel lines

title: The first hard drive weighed a tonne and held 5 MB
body: IBM's RAMAC of 1956 stored about five million characters on fifty spinning discs, each 61 cm wide. It was the size of two refrigerators. A one-terabyte memory card smaller than a fingernail holds 200,000 times more.
takeaway: Storage that once filled a room and cost a fortune is now nearly free.
visual: a 1950s cabinet with a tall stack of large spinning metal discs, beside a tiny memory card on a fingertip

title: Modern AI traces back to one 2017 paper
body: Eight Google researchers published "Attention Is All You Need", describing a design called the Transformer. It was built for translation. It is now the T in GPT and the basis of nearly every large language model.
takeaway: The idea: let every word look at every other word at once and decide which matter.
visual: a row of glowing beads with bright curved lines connecting every bead to every other bead

title: GPS only works because of Einstein
body: Clocks on GPS satellites run about 38 millionths of a second per day faster than clocks on the ground. They move fast, which slows them, and sit in weaker gravity, which speeds them up more. Uncorrected, your position would drift by about 10 km a day.
takeaway: Relativity is working in your pocket every time a map finds you.
source: Neil Ashby, "Relativity in the Global Positioning System", Living Reviews in Relativity (2003)
visual: a ring of satellites around Earth, each carrying a small glowing clock, with beams converging on one point on the ground
